Testimony In Support of

LD 1830 Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer
Dear Senator Bailey, Rep. Mathieson and fellow members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services,
I am State Representative Barbara Bagshaw, representing District 106, part of Windham. I am
sponsoring LD 1830 Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from
Cancer because of the unusually high risk of exposure to our first responders.
According to the International Association ofFirefighter 's the number one cause of death for
Firefighters is occupational cancer, with firefighters having a 9% greater risk of being diagnosed
with cancer and a 14% higher risk of dying from cancer than the general population.

Creating a screening program will help in early detection in a high-risk environment.

Thank you for your time, and I would be happy to answer any questions.

Yours truly,

Thank you in advance for considering this very important bill.
As reported by the Firefighter Cancer Support Network we know from several studies from the CDC and NIOSH that due to their work firefighters have a 9 % higher risk of being diagnosed with cancer and a 14% high risk of dying from cancer than the general U.S. Population. Some instances of cancer including mesothelioma has double the risk in firefighters. Cancer was the cause in 66% of career firefighter line-of-duty deaths between 2002 and 2019.
We have been able to take many steps in the industry to help limit exposure and ensure that we are taking preventive steps to protect ourselves and our families. If there can be any positive to a cancer diagnosis it is early detection and treatment. This bill will help to get that early detection out to our state and into the stations of our firefighters.
As a grassroots effort the fire service in Maine and the Maine Fire Chief's Association has been able to accomplish some early detection and without a doubt has saved lives because of it. Please support this bill.

Good afternoon,
My name is Max Newton and I am a firefighter/paramedic for the town of
Scarborough. I am honored to be here today to speak of the importance of
preventative cancer screenings for firefighters. Last March I had a routine preventative ultrasound performed by United Diagnostic Services. I went to the ultrasound with no symptoms and no health issues. As a result of the ultrasound a
0.9cm mass was found on my thyroid. Follow up ultrasounds and a biopsy revealed
that I had Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (Thyroid cancer). Again, I had no signs or symptoms that I had cancer and the preventative ultrasound is the only test that detected it. Since the preventative ultrasound I have undergone two surgeries (one
last Tuesday) to remove my thyroid and seven lymph nodes. I will undergo a
radioactive iodine treatment this summer to eradicate the remaining cancer cells as
the cancer has spread to my lymphatic system as well.
My case is not unique. There were at least six other firefighters that I know of that
had serious medical conditions discovered during preventative ultra sounds last
year, including one other firefighter who had the same cancer as me. It is not a stretch to say this screening saved our lives, and I still believe it is the best money I
have ever spent.

I am one of the lucky ones who had a highly treatable cancer with a very low
mortality rate when caught this early on. I was also lucky that my department
shared the availability of the preventative ultrasounds and I was able to afford the
$350 dollars for the ultrasound. There are many firefighters out there who may not be able to afford the cost of these preventative screenings. Some departments are working towards covering at least part of the cost of the screening, but many more
simply can not afford to cover these screenings.
This is especially true of many of the volunteer fire departments in Maine. For
example, at my local volunteer fire station in Readfield we use every dollar of our
budget to make sure our vehicles, equipment, and gear are functioning and ready to serve our residents. Covering the cost of the cancer screenings for our 25 members would add $8,750 to our yearly budget, roughly a ten percent increase. This may not seem like a big increase, but in small towns like Readfield and hundreds of other small towns in Maine that is a huge increase to a fire department budget.
In 2024 308 firefighters were honored at the International Association of Fire
Fighters memorial weekend, with 75% of those honored having died from
occupational cancer. This makes cancer the leading cause of death in firefighters.

Cancer prevention, including the elimination of PFAS chemicals from our gear, is
gaining more and more attention, but does not change the years of exposure that
thousands of firefighters have already encountered. Catching the early signs of
cancer in firefighters is the best way to prevent future line of duty deaths, and these preventative screenings are the best way to detect the early signs and stages of
cancer.
Thank you for hearing my story and my experience with preventative cancer
screenings.

Testimony ofSenator Rachel Talbot Ross in support of
LD 1830, "Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from
Cancer"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services
May 7, 2025
Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services, my name is Rachel Talbot Ross. I represent Senate District 28, which includes part of my hometown of Portland and Peaks Island. I am pleased to be a cosponsor and provide testimony in support of LD 1830, a "Resolve,
to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer."
As we all know, firefighters are essential in safeguarding our communities. They run toward
danger, often exposing themselves to harmful carcinogens and toxic substances that significantly increase their risk of developing cancer. Despite advancements in protective gear and training,
the nature of their work places them in high-risk situations Where their health is continually
compromised.
LD 1830 seeks to establish a pilot program that will offer comprehensive early-detection cancer
screenings to both active and retired firefighters. By providing these lifesaving screenings, we
can reduce the long-term impacts of cancer on our first responders and support their continued service to our communities.
Specifically, this resolve requires the Commissioner of Public Safety to establish a program
offering a range of screenings, including multi-cancer blood tests, ultrasounds, and CT scans,
which are essential for detecting a wide array of cancers at early, more treatable stages. This proactive approach will save lives, reduce healthcare costs, and honor our firefighters' sacrifices
every day.
Moreover, this pilot program aims to provide flexibility and choice by allowing firefighters to select the screening methods that best fit their individual needs. It also creates a committee to ensure the program is effectively administered and responsive to the evolving needs of our first
responders.
As a cosponsor of this important legislation, I urge you to support this measure to protect those who protect us. Let us stand with our firefighters by investing in their long-term health and well-
being.
Thank you for your consideration, and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
Neither for Nor Against
LD 1830 - Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer
March 7, 2025
_____________________________________________________________________________________
Sen. Bailey, Rep. Matheson and distinguished members of the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am submitting testimony neither for nor against on behalf of Maine Municipal Association for LD 1830, Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer, at the direction of our 70 member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC).
There is already an existing pilot program with vendor screenings for cancer and cardiac risk along with first responder culturally competent wellness and mental health programs as viable options under language enacted last session in Part T of the Supplemental Budget. This pilot program has recently closed for accepting applications and is moving into the award phase expected in a couple of weeks. What is missing from the current program is an avenue to take legislative action on the outcomes of the screenings and how to guarantee the ongoing availability of these options.
MMA reached out to the sponsor of this bill to ask that the resolve be shifted to accommodate the pilot program already in progress under the Office of the Fire Marshal with a reporting mechanism that would include this committee along with the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety and include authority to report out a bill in the 2nd regular session of the 132nd Legislature on recommendations resulting from the existing pilot program. We remain eager to work to provide additional amended language for the bill if desired.
What is most important about the existing screening program is that it provides screenings for fire, police, EMS, dispatch and corrections all of whom experience health related issues tied to long term exposure to traumatic events.
The LD 1830 proposed resolve is recreating the wheel for this program and narrowly defines who is able to receive the screenings. Cancer screenings for fire fighters are a vital part of the existing screening program, but more importantly, a part of the screening program for ALL first responders. The Association and its members believe these are important elements that should be maintained. Additionally, the added work for another program as drafted is unlikely to be able to be accomplished by the Department of Public Safety and would be better served by directing efforts into bolstering and continuing the existing program, adding this committee to those who should received a report on outcomes of the existing program in 2026, and provide some authority to either committee to introduce legislation based on the outcomes.

Testimony of Sarah Woodbury, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, Defend Our Health In Support of LD 1830, "Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from

Before the Environment and Natural Resources Committee

Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson and members of the Health Coverage, Insurance, ad
Financial Services Committee. My name is Sarah Woodbury. I am the vice president of policy and advocacy for Defend Our Health. Defend Our Health's mission is the make sure that
everyone has equal access to safe food and drinking water, healthy homes and products that
are toxic-free and climate friendly. I am here to testify in support of 1830, "Resolve, to Establish
a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer."
Firefighters, both career and volunteer, face unique and repeated exposures to carcinogenic materials while protecting lives and property. These exposures are cumulative and unavoidable in the line of duty. Studies consistently show that firefighters are significantly more likely than the general public to develop various forms of cancer, including cancers of the lungs, liver, bladder, prostate, and more. According to the Firefighter Cancer Support Network "Cancer caused 66 percent of the career firefighter line-of-duty deaths from 2002 to 2019, according to data from the International Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF). Heart disease caused 18 percent
of career LODDs for the same period. Firefighters have a 9 percent higher risk of being
diagnosed with cancer and a 14 percent higher risk of dying from cancer than the general U.S. population, according to research by the CDC/National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety." Early detection is our strongest line of defense.
We appreciate Rep. Bagshaw for bringing this bill forward. We do have a concern with the
language that we would urge the committee to address when moving forward with the bill. Our first concern is with who pays for the testing. The bill states that firefighters can be reimbursed
up to $1300 for any testing. That's great. However, medical testing is expensive. Depending on
the type of testing, $1300 will not be enough. Just from my personal experience, I got a bill from my doctor's office for $3200 for one cardiac MRI. Additionally, this implies they have to pay for
those tests up front and be reimbursed. That isn't financially feasible for mamy firefighters. We
don't believe that the firefighters should be required to pay for any of the testing under the pilot
program.
LD 1830 acknowledges the risks firefighters face and offers them the same commitment to safety that they give to us every day. If we can catch even a few cases of cancer early, the
program will be worth it. We urge you to vote "ought to pass" on LD 1830.

LD 1830, Resolve, to Establish a Pilot Program to Protect Firefighters from Cancer
Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and distinguished members of the Health Coverage, Insurance, and Financial Services Committee, my name is Shawn Esler, and it is a privilege to serve as the State Fire Marshal. I write in opposition of LD 1830.
We are in opposition only because this resolve duplicates an effort currently underway. Recently, the Department of Public Safety released the Public Safety Health and Wellness Reimbursement Fund (Request for Application) to reimburse government entities the cost of providing cancer, cardiovascular, and mental health screenings. Not only does our program include firefighters, but law enforcement officers, corrections, dispatchers, and EMS providers.
The Public Safety Health and Wellness Reimbursement Fund was modeled after a successful pilot program in Southern Maine that recently completed a screening, where in one example, they found a cancerous tumor. That firefighter was able to receive early medical treatment. Another screening found a massive heart block and that firefighter later received open heart surgery, likely mitigating a tragedy.
The one-time funding of $2,000,000 aims to provide all 16 counties across Maine with supplemental funding to jumpstart first responder wellness and yield results like the examples above. I encourage the Committee to learn more about this program by visiting the website of the Office of State Procurement Services. We are currently in the process of evaluating the applications and we intend to announce awards prior to July 1, 2025.
In July 2026, the Office of State Fire Marshal (FMO) will be able to create a report describing the effectiveness of the reimbursement fund. We believe through the statewide data captured over the next year; we will simultaneously accomplish the goal of LD 1830.
If additional funding is considered on an ongoing basis, the need to consider a single FMO position (Office Associate II) will be necessary. The FMO has worked to deliver this program almost entirely after hours because we simply do not have the manpower to both oversee these important programs and manage existing services.
